title: Figures of speech at a glance

head: Figure
What it does
Example
rows: compares two unlike things using 'like' or 'as'
says one thing is another, with no 'like' or 'as'
gives human actions or feelings to a thing
repeats the same first consonant sound
a word that imitates a sound
two opposite words side by side

blocks.text: Two UNLIKE things compared with 'like' or 'as' → simile; the same comparison without them → metaphor.
"Ali is as tall as his brother" is NOT a simile: it compares two things of the same kind, literally.
Guess a hard word from the words around it. Look for the clue type:

items: Contrast (unlike, but, although): the word means the opposite of the clue. "Unlike his talkative brother, Bilal was reticent" → reticent = quiet.
Restatement (that is, or, a dash or commas): the meaning is given right after.
Example (such as, for example): the examples show the meaning.
Cause and effect (so … that, because): the result explains the word.

blocks.text: Scanning for facts
Pick the key word or number from the question, find it in the passage, then read that sentence and the one around it.
An option that is true in real life but not stated in the passage is wrong. Answer only from the passage.

head: Term
What it is
Target
rows: the result or meaning is the opposite of what is expected or said
bitter, mocking irony meant to hurt: "Oh, brilliant work!" to someone who broke a glass
uses humour and exaggeration to expose the faults of society or rulers, hoping for change
a comic imitation of a particular writer, work or style

blocks.text: A column saying roads have "so many potholes that people swim in them" mocks the city government → satire.
Shades of meaning: frugal (careful, positive) vs stingy (mean, negative). Check whether the context praises or blames.

items: Since (point of time) / for (period) → present perfect. ✓ "We have known each other since 2015." ✗ "We know each other since 2015."
Interrupted action → past continuous + simple past. ✓ "While Sara was cooking, the lights went out." ✗ "While Sara cooked, the lights were going out."
After when / if / as soon as with future meaning, use the present. ✓ "I will call you when he arrives." ✗ "… when he will arrive."

head: Type
If-clause
Main clause
rows: will + verb: we will stay in.
past: If I were a bird,
had + V3: If I had known,
would have + V3: I would have studied.

blocks.text: Formal English uses 'were' for every person in type 2: ✓ "If I were" ✗ "If I would be".

items: No 'to' after make, let, had better, would rather and modals. ✓ "The teacher made us rewrite the essay." ✗ "made us to rewrite"
Passive brings 'to' back. ✓ "We were made to rewrite the essay."
-ing after enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, keep, suggest. ✓ "Sara enjoys reading novels." ✗ "enjoys to read"
When 'to' is a preposition, use -ing: look forward to, be used to, object to, with a view to. ✓ "I look forward to meeting you." ✗ "look forward to meet you"

blocks.text: A gerund is an -ing word working as a noun: "Swimming is good exercise." In "He is swimming" it is part of the verb, not a gerund.
Meaning changes: "He stopped smoking" (gave it up) vs "He stopped to smoke" (paused in order to smoke).

head: Use
Preposition
Example
rows: months, years, parts of the day
Sara was walking in the garden.

blocks.text: "walking in the garden" = already there, moving about; "walked into the garden" = entered it from outside.
When a negative or limiting word starts the sentence, use question order: helping verb + subject.

items: ✓ "Never have I seen such rain." ✗ "Never I have seen such rain."
Fixed pairs: Hardly / Scarcely … when; No sooner … than. ✓ "No sooner had the train left than it started raining." ✗ "No sooner had the train left when …"
✓ "Little did he know that his friends were planning a surprise." ✗ "Little he knew …"
If dropped: ✓ "Had I known about the test, I would have studied harder." = If I had known …

blocks.text: No inversion when the word is not first: "He had hardly sat down when the phone rang."

head: Active
Passive
rows: The fan is repaired by Ali.
The fan is being repaired by Ali.
The fan has been repaired by Ali.
Was the glass broken by Hamza?
The principal gave Bilal a prize.
Bilal was given a prize by the principal.

blocks.text: Reported speech (past reporting verb)

items: Tense moves one step back: is → was, has → had, will → would.
Question → asked if / whether + statement order, no question mark: Ali asked me if I was coming to the party.
Request or order → asked / told + to-infinitive: Fatima asked Ali to lend her his pen.

blocks.text: ✗ "Ali asked me was I coming." Reported questions never keep question order.

items: Two subjects joined by 'and' → plural pronoun. ✓ "Ayesha and Sara finished their homework." ✗ "… finished her homework."
Each / every + noun → singular pronoun and verb. ✓ "Each of the boys has his own bag." ✗ "Each of the boys have their own bag."
One clear antecedent only. ✗ "Ali told Bilal that he had passed." (who passed?) ✓ "Ali told Bilal, 'You have passed.'"
who for people, which for things. ✓ "The machine which makes the ice has broken." ✗ "The machine who makes …"

blocks.text: Adverb position

items: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after 'be' or the first helping verb. ✓ "She always arrives early." ✓ "She is always late." ✗ "She arrives always early."
'Only' goes next to what it limits: "Only Bilal passed the test" (nobody else) vs "Bilal passed only the English test" (no other test).

head: Job
Transition words
rows: however, nevertheless, on the other hand

items: Joining two full sentences with a transition: semicolon before, comma after. ✓ "Submit the form by Friday; otherwise, your admission will be cancelled." ✗ "Submit the form by Friday, otherwise your admission …"
Plural owner: apostrophe after the s. ✓ "the two students' results" ✗ "the two student's results"
its = belonging to it; it's = it is. ✓ "The cat hurt its paw." ✗ "The cat hurt it's paw."
A reported question ends with a full stop. ✓ "She asked where I lived." ✗ "She asked where I lived?"
Each / every / either / neither (of + plural) → singular verb. ✓ "Each of the students has a laptop." ✗ "Each of the students have …"
as well as, along with, together with do not make the subject plural. ✓ "The captain, as well as his players, is happy." ✗ "… are happy."
A sum of money, time or distance as one amount → singular. ✓ "Five hundred rupees is too much for this book."
Neither … nor / either … or → verb agrees with the nearer subject. ✓ "Neither the teacher nor the students were late."
The number of → singular; a number of → plural. ✓ "The number of patients has risen." ✓ "A number of patients have recovered."

blocks.text: Cross out the words between the subject and the verb, then match.

items: No preposition after discuss, reach, resemble, or enter (a place). ✓ "We discussed the plan." ✗ "We discussed about the plan."
Cope with, not 'cope up with'. ✓ "He could not cope with the pressure." ✗ "cope up with"
Hardly, scarcely and barely are already negative. ✓ "I could hardly hear the speaker." ✗ "I couldn't hardly hear."
Not only … but also: put both parts before the same kind of word. ✓ "He is not only clever but also hard-working." ✗ "He not only is clever but also hard-working."
A sentence needs a subject and a finite verb, and a 'because' clause cannot stand alone. ✗ "Because the bus was late."

blocks.text: Doubles to cut: 'return back', 'repeat again', 'reason … is because'.

head: The gap comes …
It needs
Example
rows: after 'the', 'a' or 'his', with no noun after the gap
The construction of the bridge took three years.
after an action verb, telling how

items: accommodation: double c, double m
necessary: one c, double s
receive, ceiling: i before e, except after c
occurred, beginning: double the last consonant before -ed/-ing when the stress is at the end
advice (noun) / advise (verb)

blocks.text: ✗ "She spoke so moving that …" — the gap tells how she spoke, so it needs the adverb.
